passage:
Monday. Hansa wanted to be out playing before six, so she raced through her maths homework in twenty minutes and skipped the checking. Her friend Ujjwal shouted from downstairs, and she ran.

Thursday. The teacher handed the sheet back: seven answers marked wrong for silly slips, a sign copied the wrong way and a missing zero. Hansa stared at the red marks.

Saturday. Instead of going out first, Hansa redid the seven, which took an hour, longer than checking would have. Ujjwal waited outside and said, "You lost more time this way." She nodded. On Monday she set herself a ten-minute check after finishing homework.

qa.q: How many answers were marked wrong?
qa.a: Seven answers were marked wrong.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she stared at the red marks?
qa.a: Disappointed and annoyed with herself, seeing that the slips were avoidable.

qa.q: What change did Hansa make afterwards?
qa.a: Hansa set a ten-minute check after finishing homework, before going out.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal's remark suggest about how Ujjwal saw the rushed work?
qa.a: Ujjwal saw that the rushing cost more time than a quick check would have, and said so plainly but not unkindly.

grounding: Shows a teenager rushing homework to reach leisure, making careless errors and having to redo the work.

passage: Harsha, put that phone down a moment. I'm Disha, your Nani, and I am not going to lecture you. I'm going to tell you a story. When I was fifteen, the science fair poster was due on Friday, and a cousin's wedding party started that evening. I hurried: glued the pictures crooked, wrote the title in a rush and spelled it wrong. My teacher saw it and said, "This is not your best." She gave me until Monday to redo it. I sat up two nights, cutting and gluing again, and I missed the wedding dance I had hurried for. Doing it slowly on Thursday would have been quicker than doing it twice over the weekend.

qa.q: What did Disha get wrong on the poster title?
qa.a: Disha spelled the title wrong.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling as she hurried through the poster?
qa.a: Eager and impatient to reach the wedding party, and not thinking about the mistakes.

qa.q: What turning point led Disha to redo the poster?
qa.a: The teacher said "This is not your best" and gave until Monday, so Disha redid it over two nights.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen Disha's poster?
qa.a: As rushed and below what Disha could do, and worth a kind second chance.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how hurrying to get to a party led to careless work that had to be redone.

passage:
In Edinburgh, Freya had one hour before her friends went online for their game night. Maths homework: twenty questions on percentages.
She raced. Twelve minutes in, she was on question fifteen. She didn't write the working, just the answers. She didn't check whether the question asked for the increase or the new total. At minute twenty she slammed the book shut and ran to her laptop, feeling pleased with her speed.
Her older sister Layla, marking her own essay at the kitchen table, raised an eyebrow. "Done already?"
"I'm efficient."
On Thursday the homework came back: eleven out of twenty. Six of the mistakes were the same one: she had given the increase when the question asked for the new price. Mr Ross had written, "You know how to do this. Redo 6–20, with working."
It took her fifty minutes. She missed the next game night.

qa.q: What score did Freya get on the homework?
qa.a: Eleven out of twenty.

qa.q: How did Freya feel when she slammed the book shut?
qa.a: Freya felt pleased and proud of her speed, thinking of it as being efficient.

qa.q: What could Freya do next time to avoid the redo?
qa.a: Freya could write the working and reread what each question asks before answering, even if it takes a bit longer.

qa.q: How does Layla see Freya's quick finish?
qa.a: Layla is doubtful, raising an eyebrow at "Done already?" because she suspects the speed hides mistakes.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who rushes homework for leisure, makes careless errors and ends up redoing more than she saved.

passage:
Evening study hour in the girls' hostel ended at eight, and the TV room opened at eight. Leela wanted to be there first for the new serial.
Physics numericals, ten of them. She wrote each answer fast, skipping the units. At 7:40 she closed her notebook. Her roommate Gopika was still on question four, drawing little diagrams.
"You're so slow," Leela teased, and went to get the good seat.
The next week, in the unit test, the same kind of numericals came. Leela wrote them just as fast. When the papers came back, she had lost nine marks: units missing, one decimal in the wrong place, one answer copied wrong from her rough work. Gopika had lost two.
The warden announced that anyone below sixty would sit a retest on Sunday morning. Leela was at fifty-eight.
On Sunday, while others slept, Leela sat in the empty study hall writing units after every answer.

qa.q: How many marks did Leela lose in the unit test?
qa.a: She had lost nine marks.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she teased Gopika?
qa.a: Leela felt smug and pleased with herself, sure that finishing fast meant she was doing well.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Leela change?
qa.a: Leela skipped units and checking to save time; writing units and checking once before closing the book would save the marks.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt when the papers came back?
qa.a: Gopika probably felt quietly relieved and satisfied, since her slow, careful work lost only two marks.

grounding: Shows a teenager who rushes through work to get to leisure and loses marks and a Sunday to careless errors.

passage:
Dear Vaibhav bhaiya,
You asked how the prelims went. The truth is embarrassing.
I finished the maths paper forty minutes early. I was so proud. I sat there drawing on the question paper while everyone else was still writing. I thought, I'm just faster than them.
Then the results came. I lost fourteen marks. Not because I didn't know things. I copied a 6 as a 0. I forgot a minus sign. I answered part (a) of a question and never saw part (b) on the next page. Ma'am wrote at the top, "Careless, not weak."
That hurt more than a low mark would have.
You always told me to use the last fifteen minutes to check. I thought that was for slow people. It turns out checking is the fast way, because now I have to redo the whole chapter test.
Next time I'll stay in my seat till the bell.
Your sister,
Mehak

qa.q: How many marks did Mehak lose in the maths paper?
qa.a: I lost fourteen marks.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel about "Careless, not weak"?
qa.a: Mehak felt hurt and ashamed, more than a low mark would have caused, because the mistakes came from rushing.

qa.q: What does Mehak plan to do next time, and why?
qa.a: Mehak plans to stay till the bell and check, because checking turns out to be faster than redoing the whole chapter test.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Vaibhav might feel sympathetic, and a little pleased that his advice about checking is finally being taken.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who rushes through an exam to finish fast and loses marks to careless errors.

passage:
Okay, Kalyani, don't laugh. Remember Thursday, when I finished the physics worksheet in fifteen minutes? I was so proud. Cricket was starting at six on the colony ground and I wanted to bat first. So I zipped through: wrote the formulas, plugged in numbers, didn't check units, didn't read question seven properly. Done. Out the door.
Today Sir gave them back. Eleven out of twenty. In question three I wrote force in kilograms. Question seven asked for time and I gave speed. The worst part? I knew all of it. Sir circled the answers and wrote, "You know this. Slow down." Now I have to redo the whole sheet by Monday, so those fifteen minutes have turned into an evening. And I got out for four runs anyway. That's me, Gurpreet, the fastest finisher in class ten, with the marks to show for it.

qa.q: What score did Gurpreet get on the worksheet?
qa.a: Eleven out of twenty.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel on Thursday compared with today?
qa.a: On Thursday Gurpreet felt proud and eager to get to cricket; today Gurpreet feels frustrated and a bit embarrassed, since every answer was within reach.

qa.q: What small step could Gurpreet take before rushing out next time?
qa.a: Spend a couple of minutes rereading each question and checking the units before closing the book.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Gurpreet's worksheet?
qa.a: The teacher sees someone who knows the work but rushed it, which is why the note says "You know this. Slow down."

grounding: Shows a teenager hurrying through homework to get to play, making careless errors that cost marks and a redo.
